title: THE WOMAN WHO SAVED MOSES BEFORE PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER DID
paragraphs: THE WOMAN WHO SAVED MOSES BEFORE PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER DID
History remembers the princess.
Heaven remembers the mother.
Most people know the dramatic scene. A helpless infant floating among the reeds of the Nile. A compassionate royal daughter discovering him. A child destined to confront kings and split seas.
But long before Pharaoh's daughter ever laid eyes on Moses, another woman stood between him and death.
A woman whose name is often spoken quietly.
A woman whose courage changed the history of redemption.
A woman whose faith protected a deliverer before the world even knew he existed.
Her name was Jochebed.
And if we are honest, her story feels painfully familiar.
Because there are moments when every believer finds themselves standing where Jochebed stood—trapped between impossible circumstances and impossible promises.
The story begins in darkness.
Egypt had become a place of terror for God's covenant people. What began as a season of favor under Joseph had become generations of oppression. Fear ruled the throne.
Pharaoh looked upon the growing Hebrew population and saw not neighbors but threats.
Exodus 1 records one of the most horrifying decrees in Scripture:
"Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river."
This was not merely political oppression.
It was attempted annihilation.
It was state-sponsored murder.
It was an attack against the covenant promises God had given to Abraham centuries earlier.
The enemy knew something was coming.
The enemy always attacks what God intends to use.
And somewhere in the middle of that national nightmare, a Hebrew woman discovered she was carrying a child.
Imagine the fear.
Imagine feeling life move inside your womb while knowing the government had already signed your son's death warrant.
Imagine hearing other mothers weep.
Imagine hearing stories of babies stolen.
Imagine counting the months until birth while wondering whether your child would survive.
Yet Scripture introduces her with stunning simplicity.
Exodus 2:1-2 tells us:
"And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months."
The Greek translation of the Old Testament, known as the Septuagint, uses language emphasizing that the child was beautiful and remarkable.
Hebrews 11:23 later explains what was really happening:
"By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents."
By faith.
Not luck.
Not instinct.
Faith.
The Greek word used here is πίστις (pistis), meaning trust, confidence, and unwavering reliance upon God.
Jochebed looked at circumstances that screamed death and chose to trust a God who promised life.
Faith does not deny reality.
Faith simply believes God has the final word about reality.
For three months she hid her son.
Every cry could expose him.
Every knock on the door could end everything.
Every day required courage.
Faith is rarely loud.
Most of the time it looks like surviving another day.
It looks like praying another prayer.
It looks like obeying when your hands are shaking.
It looks like trusting God while your heart is breaking.
Eventually she could hide him no longer.
This is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Exodus says she prepared an ark of bulrushes.
The Hebrew word used is תֵּבָה (tevah).
Remarkably, this exact word appears only one other time in the entire Old Testament.
Noah's ark.
That is not accidental.
When judgment covered the earth, God preserved Noah through an ark.
When death threatened Moses, God preserved him through an ark.
The same God who saved Noah was saving Moses.
The same God who preserved the covenant before was preserving it again.
Jochebed coated the basket with pitch.
Placed her son inside.
And carried him toward the Nile.
Try to imagine the weight of those steps.
Every mother understands that some moments break your heart simply because love is involved.
This was not abandonment.
This was surrender.
Not surrender to fate.
Surrender to God.
She could no longer protect him herself.
So she entrusted him to the One who could.
That is often the hardest faith of all.
Not trusting God when you still have options.
Trusting God when your options have run out.
Many believers are standing at their own Nile River right now.
A marriage they cannot fix.
A child they cannot rescue.
A diagnosis they cannot change.
A burden they cannot carry.
A future they cannot control.
And like Jochebed, they are discovering that sometimes faith means placing what you love most into God's hands.
The Nile was supposed to be a place of death.
Instead it became a pathway to destiny.
That is how God works.
What the enemy designs as destruction often becomes divine transportation.
The river Pharaoh intended to kill Hebrew sons became the very river that carried Israel's future deliverer into the palace.
The irony is breathtaking.
God often defeats evil using the very mechanisms evil created.
Then comes the moment everyone remembers.
Pharaoh's daughter discovers the child.
Her heart is moved with compassion.
She chooses mercy over policy.
Life over law.
And in one of Scripture's most astonishing reversals, Moses' own mother is hired to raise him.
Only God could write a story like that.
The woman who surrendered her son receives him back.
The woman who trusted God is entrusted with the very child she feared losing.
The woman who risked everything watches God do what she never could.
This is not merely a story about motherhood.
It is a story about redemption.
Because Jochebed's story points beyond Moses.
It points to Jesus.
Every great story in Scripture eventually leads us to Christ.
Moses would become a deliverer.
Jesus would become the Deliverer.
Moses would lead people out of slavery.
Jesus would lead humanity out of sin.
Moses would confront Pharaoh.
Jesus would confront death itself.
Moses would guide Israel through water.
Jesus would open the way to eternal life.
And just as God preserved Moses to accomplish salvation history, God preserved the line through which the Messiah would eventually come.
Nothing could stop God's redemptive plan.
Not Pharaoh.
Not oppression.
Not genocide.
Not fear.
Not rivers.
Not kingdoms.
Not hell itself.
The Gospel is filled with this same pattern.
What looks like defeat becomes victory.
What looks like scandal becomes grace.
What looks like an ending becomes a beginning.
The cross itself appeared to be history's greatest failure.
The Son of God rejected.
Beaten.
Mocked.
Crucified.
Buried.
Yet three days later the empty tomb revealed what heaven knew all along.
God was rewriting everything.
The very instrument of execution became the symbol of salvation.
The place of shame became the place of redemption.
The scandal became grace.
That is why Jochebed's story still matters.
Because every believer eventually discovers that God does some of His greatest work in moments that feel completely out of control.
The Nile was never outside God's sovereignty.
Neither is your situation.
The thing keeping you awake at night is not bigger than the God who carried Moses through the reeds.
The chapter confusing you is not beyond the Author's ability to rewrite.
The wound is not beyond healing.
The failure is not beyond redemption.
The shame is not beyond grace.
The story is not over.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You have been staring at a river and calling it the end.
God sees a pathway.
You have been staring at a basket and calling it loss.
God sees preservation.
You have been staring at uncertainty and calling it fear.
God sees preparation.
You have been staring at a scandal.
God already sees grace.
If this story stirred something deep inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
What is the "Nile River" in your life that you are struggling to place into God's hands?
Be honest.
Someone else may find hope through your testimony.

Faithful support helps spread biblical truth, create more Christ-centered resources, and reach people who desperately need the Gospel. If we truly desire to glorify God with what He has entrusted to us, supporting Gospel-centered work and sharing it publicly becomes part of that stewardship.
Because somewhere right now, another Jochebed is praying through tears.
And somewhere right now, God is already moving through the reeds.
The river never had the final word.
Jesus did.
